text: The ongoing 2026 case provides a real-time comparison: after far-eastern/eastern Pacific SST warming begins, do low-level winds, sea-level pressure, rainfall, and convection respond at the same time? ERA5 indicates that wind and pressure begin to recover in spring, while rainfall and convection remain the slowest branch.

name: note-4-body
text:
Dataset: NOAA OISST v2.1 monthly SST anomaly.

Key reading: after February 2026, FEP and Niño1+2 warming intensifies rapidly. A positive FEP residual means coastal eastern-Pacific warming is stronger than the broader tropical-Pacific background.

Role in the story: first establish that the ocean branch moved, then test whether the atmosphere responded synchronously.

name: note-5-body
text:
Datasets: OISST SST anomaly and GPCP monthly precipitation anomaly.

Key reading: MAM and Apr-May show clear eastern-Pacific/FEP warming, but the rainfall enhancement is displaced toward the western Pacific and north of the equator. A continuous positive equatorial central-eastern Pacific rainfall band is absent.

New contribution: transfer the 2023/24 SST-rainfall asynchrony question to a real-time 2026 case.

name: note-6-body
text:
Dataset: CPC Blended OLR daily anomaly averaged over selected periods.

Key reading: negative OLR means stronger deep convection; positive OLR means suppressed convection. In spring 2026, enhanced convection is displaced toward the western/northern central Pacific rather than forming a broad equatorial central-eastern Pacific signal.

Role: this gives an independent check on the rainfall conclusion.

name: note-7-body
text:
Datasets: ERA5 10 m wind anomaly and mean sea-level pressure anomaly.

Key reading: in MAM and Apr-May, westerly anomalies emerge over the central-western equatorial Pacific, and pressure lowers over the central-eastern tropical Pacific. The Tahiti-Darwin contrast becomes more El Nino-like.

Update from the older view: NCEP only covered Jan-Feb, so it showed early asynchrony. ERA5 Jan-May indicates lagged recovery rather than persistent non-response.

name: note-8-body
text:
Datasets: ERA5 total precipitation, 850 hPa zonal wind, and 850 hPa pressure velocity.

Key reading: u850 turns westerly in MAM/Apr-May, indicating that the low-level wind branch is catching up. However, rainfall remains displaced westward/northward, and central-Pacific omega850 does not show a stable strong upward-motion response.

Main conclusion: the wind-pressure branch recovers before the rainfall-convection branch.

name: note-9-body
text:
Datasets: ERA5 equatorial-mean u10, u850, precipitation, and omega850 anomalies.

Key reading: January-February shows clear central-Pacific easterly anomalies. From March to May, central-western Pacific winds gradually turn westerly. Rainfall remains broadly weak from January to April and becomes more locally positive only in May.

This is the most direct evidence for staged recovery rather than all-season decoupling.

name: right-callout-body
text: With ERA5 through May, the conclusion becomes more nuanced: early asynchrony is real, but wind and pressure begin to recover toward an El Nino-like state in March-May. The most important branch to track next is rainfall, OLR, and vertical motion, which still show lagged, northward, or fragmented responses.

name: next-step-bullets
text:
• Wait for the June 2026 ERA5 monthly mean to construct formal AMJ 2026, rather than using MAM or Apr-May as proxies.
• Insert ERA5 wind-pressure diagnostics into the existing response-ratio / observed-vs-expected framework for direct 2023-versus-2026 comparison.
• Recalculate 2023/24 AMJ/JJA using the same ERA5 variables to avoid dataset-dependent interpretation.
• Add 200 hPa divergence or velocity potential to diagnose the upper branch of the Walker circulation.
• Keep both OLR and GPCP constraints to test whether convection/rainfall shifts from west/north displacement toward the equatorial central-eastern Pacific.
